title: Dawn of a new era for Supernova 1987A
caption: Supernova 1987A, imaged by ALMA, the Hubble Space Telescope and the Chandra X-ray Observatory
celestial: SN 1987A · constellation Dorado · about 170000 light-years away (source figure)

recognition.text: ESO Picture of the Week (an editorial selection, not an audience score).

story: This composite image shows the remains of SN 1987A, a supernova in the Large Magellanic Cloud, a satellite galaxy of the Milky Way. It combines observations from ALMA, the NASA/ESA Hubble Space Telescope and NASA's Chandra X-ray Observatory.

The explosion was discovered on 23 February 1987. It was one of the brightest supernovae seen in more than 400 years, blazing for several months with the power of 100 million suns. As the nearest supernova observed in centuries, it quickly became the most thoroughly studied of all time. Decades of follow-up from space and the ground have let astronomers trace a massive star's death step by step, from star to supernova to remnant.

For several years now, ALMA has been studying the glowing debris in high resolution at millimetre and submillimetre wavelengths. It shows the remnant forming vast amounts of dust from new elements made in the original star.
scale: Using the source's listed field of view (0.11 x 0.11 arcminutes) and distance (170000 light years), the frame spans roughly 5.4 × 5.4 light-years. Its light set out about 170,000 years before reaching the telescope.

understand.summary: This composite combines millimetre-wave data from ALMA, visible light from Hubble and X-rays from Chandra. The colour assigned to each dataset is not published.
understand.eye: X-rays and millimetre waves are completely invisible to the eye, so much of what appears here could never be seen directly.

explore: Some of this dust will drift into interstellar space and may one day become material for planets around other stars. The findings hint that similar explosions produced the dust of the early Universe.
